title: The chains just automated the wrong end of the restaurant
summary: Taco Bell runs voice AI at 890+ drive-thrus and SoundHound just partnered with Deliverect. What independent operators should copy, and what to ignore.
body_text: Key takeaways Taco Bell now runs voice AI at more than 890 drive-thrus across 38 states. That is one of the biggest automation rollouts the quick-service world has seen. On July 23, SoundHound AI and Deliverect announced a partnership to push voice orders straight into kitchen systems. Deliverect connects to more than 80,000 restaurant locations and 550 point-of-sale systems. Almost all of this money is aimed at the drive-thru lane. Most independent restaurants do not have a drive-thru lane. The channel you are actually losing money on is the phone , and it is the one the chains automated first when they had no lane to fix. ‍ Two weeks of headlines have been telling independent operators they are falling behind on AI. Almost every one of them describes a problem you do not have. The first job I ever had was answering the phone in my parents' restaurant. I was nine. They started with one place and grew it to eleven, and every dinner rush looked identical. Packed dining room, everyone in the weeds, phone ringing off the wall. Somebody had to choose between the guest standing in front of them and the guest trying to spend money down the line, and the phone always lost. So when I read that Taco Bell now runs voice AI at more than 890 drive-thrus, my first thought was not that we are behind. It was that a lot of money just went into fixing a problem I never had. Let me explain what happened, and then what it actually means for you. ‍ What actually got announced this month Two things, four days apart. First, Taco Bell confirmed its voice AI is now live at more than 890 drive-thru locations across 38 states, built with a company called Omilia. It has been running at hundreds of stores since 2023. This July it crossed into nearly a thousand. Second, on July 23, SoundHound AI announced a partnership with Deliverect. Deliverect is the integration layer a lot of restaurants already use to move orders between apps and their till. It reaches over 80,000 restaurant locations, connects to more than 550 point-of-sale systems in 50-plus countries, and handles 100-plus languages. The deal lets a voice agent pull live menu data from Deliverect and drop the finished order into the kitchen automatically. Don MacMillan, who runs partnerships in the US and Canada for Deliverect, said the quiet part out loud in the announcement: "Voice is the oldest ordering channel in the restaurant business, and until now it's been the least automated." He is right. That sentence is the whole story, and almost everyone read it backwards. ‍ Why every big rollout points at the drive-thru Follow the money and it makes sense. A large chain measures itself on cars per hour. Shave eight seconds off an order across 890 stores and you have a number you can put in an earnings deck. Taco Bell's own reporting says transactions at voice-AI lanes run the same speed or faster than a person taking the order, and that those stores have seen better employee retention. Now look at it from the vendor's side, because this is the part nobody says out loud. One chain contract delivers 890 locations from a single signature. Reaching 890 independents means 890 separate sales conversations with 890 owners who all want to see it work first. If you are building a voice AI company, you already know which of those two you are going to chase. So the product gets built for the lane, and the case studies get written about the lane, and the trade press covers the lane. That is not a conspiracy, it is just how enterprise software gets funded. But it means the roadmap you have been reading about for two weeks was never written with your restaurant in mind. Burger King has been piloting an assistant across roughly 500 restaurants. Wendy's runs its own system in hundreds of locations. White Castle has gone wide with it. The pattern repeats because the problem repeats: a lane, a speaker, a queue of cars. Now go stand in your own dining room and ask what your equivalent is. For most independents there is no lane. There is a phone on the wall that rings during the exact 90 minutes nobody on your team can pick it up. ‍ The channel you are actually losing Here is the part that annoys me about the coverage. Every article treats the drive-thru as the frontier and the phone as a leftover. For an independent it is the reverse. Your phone carries the orders with the highest value in the building. Catering calls start on the phone. Big family takeout orders start on the phone. Someone asking whether you can do a table of 14 on Saturday starts on the phone. Those are not $9 tickets, and they almost never arrive through an app. Boardwalk Pizza captured over $70,000 in orders that had been slipping away on unanswered calls, and freed up 195 hours of staff time doing it. Manhattan Deli and Grill added $30,000 a month . Those numbers did not come from making a line move faster. They came from picking up a phone that used to ring out. I used to think the phone was just a cost of doing business, so I know how easy that assumption is to hold. We would let it ring during a rush and tell ourselves the good customers would call back. Some did. I have no idea how many did not, and that is exactly the problem: a missed call leaves no trace in your till. You cannot see the hole, so you never fix it. ‍ What the Deliverect deal really signals Ignore the two brand names for a second and look at the shape of the thing. A voice platform plugged itself into an order-routing layer that already touches 80,000 locations and 550 tills. That is not a product launch, it is a distribution move. It means voice ordering is about to stop being a custom build for chains with an engineering team, and start being something that arrives through infrastructure you may already be paying for. The window where "we have voice AI and our competitor doesn't" is a real advantage is closing. Not this year, probably not next. But it is closing, and the operators who set this up while it is still unusual will have a year or two of collecting orders their neighbours are still dropping. ‍ What I would do this month Four things, and none of them require a budget meeting. Count what you are missing. Call your own restaurant at 7pm on a Friday from a number your staff will not recognise. Then do it again on Saturday. If it rings out or lands in voicemail, you have your answer, and it costs you nothing to find out. Work out what one missed call is worth. Take your average takeout ticket and multiply it by the calls you just watched go unanswered. Then multiply by 30. Most operators I show this to go quiet for a second. Check whether your till can even accept a phone order automatically. Certus AI works with all major POS systems including Toast, Square, Clover, Skytab, and Aloha NCR , so orders land in the kitchen the same way a server would enter them. If a system cannot do that, you are just moving the typing to someone else. Cover Spanish properly. Certus answers in English and Spanish and switches automatically based on the caller. In a lot of neighbourhoods that alone is the difference between taking an order and losing one. We charge flat monthly pricing, set up the same day, and back it with a 30-day money-back guarantee. Our Trustpilot rating is 4.5 stars. If you want the longer comparison of what is out there, I have written up the best SoundHound alternatives for restaurants and an honest breakdown of Loman AI . ‍ The bit nobody in the trade press will say The chains are not smarter than you. They are better instrumented. They found their biggest leak because they count cars, and a slow lane shows up in a report every single morning until somebody fixes it. Your biggest leak shows up nowhere, because a phone that rings out generates no data at all. No ticket, no timestamp, no line item, nothing. You cannot manage a number that was never recorded. That is the whole distance between your restaurant and an 890-store rollout, and it is a measurement gap rather than a money one. Two phone calls this Friday will tell you how wide yours is. Nobody in the trade press will write a word about it when you close it, and your bank account will not care. ‍ About the author I'm Gurveer Singh, co-founder and CEO of Certus AI. I grew up in my family's restaurants and was helping manage 11 of them by 17, from takeaway counters to a brewery. I started Certus because the phone was the one part of the operation nobody had fixed, and it was quietly costing us more than anything on the menu. ‍ References Deliverect and SoundHound AI partnership announcement, July 23, 2026 - stocktitan.net "Taco Bell's drive-thru voice AI expands to nearly 900 restaurants," Nation's Restaurant News, July 2026 - nrn.com "Taco Bell Now Has Drive-Thru AI Ordering in About 900 Locations," QSR Magazine, July 2026 - qsrmagazine.com "Taco Bell Expands Drive-Thru Voice AI to Nearly 900 Restaurants Across the U.S.," Restaurant Technology News, July 2026 - restauranttechnologynews.com ‍

title: The Inversion: What PE Selects For vs What Actually Predicts
summary: The market knowledge your talent decisions depend on — centralized. Verata unifies company intelligence, executive data, and search management in one platform built for PE talent and executive search.
body_text: The data sorts CEO traits into three distinct categories, and the taxonomy is revealing. Category 1: Seniority proxies only. These traits predict nothing beyond what years-of-experience already captures. Prior CEO title (OR 1.07, not significant after controlling for experience) and board experience fall here. They are signals of seniority, not signals of capability. Category 2: Heavily selected, no signal. Operations (69% prevalence, OR crosses 1.0), Tech (50% prevalence, OR 0.98), Sales (31% prevalence, OR not significant), MBA (35% prevalence, OR 1.10 -- nominally positive but does not survive FDR correction). These are the traits that dominate PE search mandates. They are also the traits with the weakest empirical support. The industry's revealed preference is for traits that produce no measurable differentiation. Category 3: The dead zone. FAANG pedigree (OR 0.82, not significant), specific sector matches, and other narrow credentials. Low prevalence, no signal, and in some cases a trend toward negative association. The one exception that proves the rule: Finance background (14% prevalence) is FDR significant -- a trait the industry does not aggressively select for, yet one that shows a real statistical relationship with exits. The inversion is nearly perfect: the traits pursued most intensely carry no signal, while a trait largely ignored in search mandates carries one of the stronger effects. The two traits that actually survive full statistical correction -- general management breadth and years of accumulated experience -- are rarely the headline criteria in a search mandate. They are background noise in a process optimized for foreground credentials that do not predict.

title: Does Medicare Have Limitations on Hospital Stays?
body_text: Does Medicare Have Limitations on Hospital Stays? By Daniel Petkevich Mar 15, 2024 Medicare Part A provides coverage for hospital inpatient care, but it is subject to certain limitations. Once you have used up your Medicare Part A hospital inpatient days, you may be responsible for covering the costs of any additional inpatient care you receive during the same benefit period. Speak with a Medicare Advocate Talk to one of our Licensed Medicare Agents today to find the right plans for you. Here's a breakdown of what happens when you exhaust your Medicare Part A hospital inpatient days: Benefit Period: Medicare Part A measures your hospital coverage based on benefit periods. A benefit period begins the day you're admitted to a hospital or skilled nursing facility and ends when you've been out of the hospital or skilled nursing facility for 60 consecutive days. If you're readmitted after the end of a benefit period, a new benefit period begins, and you will have a new set of inpatient hospital days available. Costs After Using Inpatient Days: Once you've used up your allotted inpatient hospital days within a benefit period (90 days), Medicare Part A coverage for inpatient care typically stops. You may be responsible for all hospital costs during this period, including room and board, medical services, and supplies. Sixty 'reserve' days per lifetime may be used if needed) However, Medicare Part B may still cover certain outpatient services and medical supplies. Part A Deductible and Coinsurance: Medicare Part A also has deductible and coinsurance amounts you may need to pay. There is a deductible for each benefit period and coinsurance amounts for extended hospital stays. These amounts may change annually, so checking with Medicare or your healthcare provider for the most up-to-date information is important. Medicare Advantage Plans: If you have a Medicare Advantage plan (Part C), your coverage for inpatient hospital care may differ from Original Medicare (Parts A and B). Some Medicare Advantage plans offer additional benefits or different cost-sharing arrangements, so reviewing your plan's terms and conditions is essential. Medigap/Supplement Plans: If you have a Medicare Supplement (Medigap) plan, it can fill in some gaps in your Original Medicare (Parts A and B). For example, Medigap Plan G will extend your Part A coinsurance up to 365 days, cover you hospital deductible, and skilled nursing co-pays. Out-of-Pocket Costs: If you need extended inpatient hospital care and no longer have Medicare Part A days available, you may have to pay for these services out of pocket unless you have other supplemental insurance coverage. It's crucial to understand your Medicare coverage and its limitations. If you anticipate needing extended hospital care or have specific healthcare needs, it's a good idea to explore additional coverage options, such as Medicare Supplement Insurance (Medigap) policies, to help offset some of the out-of-pocket costs associated with inpatient care. title: Nike Debuts Jordan Chiles and Skye Blakely Leotard Collections
summary: Nike is expanding its commitment to the future of gymnastics with the introduction of new leotard collections from elite gymnasts, two-time Olympian Jordan Chiles and two-time World Team Champion Skye Blakely.
body_text: Nike is expanding its commitment to the future of gymnastics with the introduction of new leotard collections from elite gymnasts, two-time Olympian Jordan Chiles and two-time World Team Champion Skye Blakely. Developed alongside partner GK Elite, the collections translate athlete-inspired design into training- and competition-ready apparel while making signature styles more accessible to young gymnasts. Designed for athletes who train, compete and express themselves through movement, the collections reflect a new chapter for gymnastics — one where performance, storytelling and individuality are equally celebrated. Both Jordan and Skye played an active role in shaping their leotards from conception to completion. Jordan drew inspiration from fashion, entertainment and bold visual storytelling, emphasizing a prominent Swoosh and dynamic design details, including a one-legged silhouette inspired by Florence Griffith Joyner’s iconic track style. Her collection reflects the confidence, strength and competitive mindset she brings to the sport every day. Skye brought original sketches and a softer creative lens to her collection, pairing feminine color palettes with striking visual execution. The result is a design that balances elegance with performance while reflecting her personal style on and off the competition floor. Throughout development, both athletes worked alongside Nike and GK Elite to provide feedback on fit, materials, trims and functionality — refining every detail to ensure the leotards perform at the highest level while preserving each athlete’s unique creative vision. Each silhouette tells a distinct story while celebrating the qualities that define today’s gymnasts: confidence, precision, power and individuality. Athlete signatures appear on every leotard, creating a personal connection between the designs and the athletes who inspired them. Thoughtfully placed graphics, color blocking and performance materials combine to create collections that feel equally at home during competition, training and everyday wear. The collections also reflect a broader evolution within gymnastics, where athletes increasingly influence culture through personal style, storytelling and self-expression alongside their athletic achievements. By combining technical performance with athlete-led design, the collections empower young gymnasts to see themselves reflected in what they wear — and to train with confidence inspired by two of the sport’s most recognizable athletes. The Jordan Chiles and Skye Blakely leotard collections will be available in kids' XS through adult XL sizing beginning July 15 at nike.com and gkelite.com .

title: Best Ear Protection for Shooting in 2026 — Range, Competition & Tactical
summary: A short training session or recreational trip to an indoor range without effective and properly worn ear protection can easily cause permanent or even short-term hearing damage. Firearms produce impulse noise between 140 and 175 decibels, far exceeding the 85 dB threshold considered safe for human hearing. Whether you're a first-time range visitor, a recreational/competitive shooter, or training in a tactical environment, choosing the correct hearing protection is critical. What makes hearing protection critical can require a substantial amount of research. The good news? There are options for every scenario including, from inexpensive foam ear plugs to advanced electronic systems that let you hear conversations while blocking hazardous noise levels. In this guide, we'll take a deep dive into the best ear protection for shooting, explain how much you actually need, and assist in choosing the right setup for your specific use case. How Loud Is Shooting? (Why This Matters) Gunfire is not just loud, it can be dangerously loud and harmful to your ears. Here's a breakdown of common firearm noise levels: ~125 dB Suppressed 9mm Most common defensive handgun cartridge for law enforcement, military, and civilian self defense. ~140 dB .22 LR Rifle Extremely common for recreational shooting (plinking). ~165 dB .223/5.56 AR-15 Most common sporting rifle for match and recreational shooting as well as varmint hunting. ~165 dB 12-Gauge Shotgun Law enforcement and sporting, hunting, and home defense applications. ~170 dB .308 Rifle Most popular cartridge for hunting white tail deer, with military and law enforcement applications. Anything above 140 dB can cause immediate, irreversible hearing damage. Indoor ranges are even worse due to sound reflecting off of walls, increasing noise levels by an additional 5–10 dB, making proper protection even more critical, particularly with rifles and larger calibers. Types of Ear Protection for Shooting Foam Ear Plugs NRR 28–33 28–33. They are economical and widely available, making them a great option for beginners or as a backup. They are worn by being inserted into the ear canal where they expand and block all sound, including important range commands and other cues — a safety and awareness consideration when in a stall with limited peripheral vision. Shop Foam Plugs → Reusable Ear Plugs NRR 22–28 A step up in durability and comfort with generally higher quality than standard foam plugs. They're ideal for plinkers on a budget, but like foam plugs, they still block out all ambient sound, restricting awareness and communication. Shop Reusable Plugs → Passive Ear Muffs NRR 22–30 Passive ear muffs provide 22–30 NRR and are faster and easier to put on and take off, making them popular for beginners and casual shooters. The downside is bulk and lack of sound awareness — not optimal for communication, and may cause issues when shouldering a long gun properly. Shop Passive Muffs → Electronic Ear Muffs NRR 22–28 Electronic muffs combine protection with awareness for optimal communication in the field and on the range. They block harmful noise while amplifying safe sounds. Best for instructors, frequent shooters, and range environments like competition or training. Shop Electronic Muffs → Electronic In-Ear NRR 18–25 Electronic ear plugs are the newest and most advanced option available and also come with the most features. Bluetooth, directional hearing, low-profile fit. Ideal for competition shooters and tactical use where mobility and spatial awareness are critical. Shop Electronic In-Ear → Best Ear Protection by Shooting Context Indoor Range Foam plugs + electronic muffs The most hazardous environment due to sound reflection. Doubling up is strongly recommended. Even if muffs are knocked off during training, plugs provide a last line of defense. Outdoor Range Electronic muffs or plugs NRR 22+ Sound dissipates more naturally, but gunshot reports remain potentially damaging. Electronic options give protection while maintaining communication and spatial awareness. Competition Shooting Electronic in-ear plugs Speed and awareness are top priorities. Rapid physical movement and sweat moisture are additional factors. Electronic in-ear provides secure fit, low profile, and clear hearing of range officer commands. Tactical / LE Training Electronic in-ear with Bluetooth / comms Communication and situational awareness are critical. These systems allow seamless team coordination while protecting hearing and enabling directional awareness for early threat detection. NRR Ratings Explained — How Much Protection Do You Actually Need? The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) tells you how much sound a device can block, but real-world performance can be lower than advertised. NRR Rating Formula Real-World Reduction NRR 22 (22 – 7) ÷ 2 ~7.5 dB NRR 25 (25 – 7) ÷ 2 ~9 dB NRR 28 (28 – 7) ÷ 2 ~10.5 dB NRR 33 (33 – 7) ÷ 2 ~13 dB This is why higher NRR and sometimes doubling up can be necessary and a best practice. Doubling Up — When and How to Wear Plugs + Muffs Doubling up means wearing ear plugs + ear muffs together. When to Do It Indoor ranges Shooting high-caliber rifles Long shooting sessions Important: NRR values don't stack directly. Instead, add about +5 dB to the higher-rated protection. Also consider that hearing protection can be uncomfortable and there is an adjustment period when someone is new to shooting. New shooters should make it a point to wear hearing protection before going to the range to get used to the slight discomfort in a non-hazardous noise environment. FAQ What is the best ear protection for shooting? This depends greatly on the environment. Indoor ranges require maximum protection (doubling up), while outdoor and competition shooting benefit from electronic options. Hearing protection should be tested off the range beforehand and phased into gradually, starting with smaller caliber firearms. Consideration should be made for the level of training, type of firearm, and environment. How much ear protection do I need for shooting? Outdoor: Minimum NRR 22. Indoor: NRR 28+ (preferably doubled). The more hazardous the environment, the higher the protection required. Can shooting damage hearing with ear protection? Yes, if your protection is insufficient for the noise level or not worn correctly. Damage can also occur if hearing protection is unintentionally moved out of place during live-fire training or competition. Are electronic ear muffs worth it? Absolutely. They allow you to hear conversations and commands while still protecting your hearing. They also provide next-gen options like text and phone call communications, as well as music playback (not recommended during live-fire training). The Axil MXII Pro covers all of the needs for recreational and competition shooting and is used around the world by experienced shooters needing optimal performance and protection. Conclusion Choosing the best ear protection for shooting has different factors, but matching your gear to your environment should be heavily considered. Indoor ranges → maximum protection (double up) Outdoor shooting → balance protection and awareness Competition/tactical → prioritize communication and mobility Modern options — especially electronic hearing protection like the Axil MXII or the XCOR Pro — make it easier than ever to stay safe without sacrificing performance. Having the best ear protection for the job allows shooters to maximize training value and optimize performance in competition. For professionals in law enforcement the stakes can be much higher. The information in this guide can assist all levels of shooters make the best decision to cover their needs and ensure the best protection, regardless of the environment.

Here's a breakdown of common firearm noise levels: ~125 dB Suppressed 9mm Most common defensive handgun cartridge for law enforcement, military, and civilian self defense. ~140 dB .22 LR Rifle Extremely common for recreational shooting (plinking). ~165 dB .223/5.56 AR-15 Most common sporting rifle for match and recreational shooting as well as varmint hunting. ~165 dB 12-Gauge Shotgun Law enforcement and sporting, hunting, and home defense applications. ~170 dB .308 Rifle Most popular cartridge for hunting white tail deer, with military and law enforcement applications. Anything above 140 dB can cause immediate, irreversible hearing damage. Indoor ranges are even worse due to sound reflecting off of walls, increasing noise levels by an additional 5–10 dB, making proper protection even more critical, particularly with rifles and larger calibers. Types of Ear Protection for Shooting Foam Ear Plugs NRR 28–33 28–33. They are economical and widely available, making them a great option for beginners or as a backup. They are worn by being inserted into the ear canal where they expand and block all sound, including important range commands and other cues — a safety and awareness consideration when in a stall with limited peripheral vision. Shop Foam Plugs → Reusable Ear Plugs NRR 22–28 A step up in durability and comfort with generally higher quality than standard foam plugs. They're ideal for plinkers on a budget, but like foam plugs, they still block out all ambient sound, restricting awareness and communication. Shop Reusable Plugs → Passive Ear Muffs NRR 22–30 Passive ear muffs provide 22–30 NRR and are faster and easier to put on and take off, making them popular for beginners and casual shooters. The downside is bulk and lack of sound awareness — not optimal for communication, and may cause issues when shouldering a long gun properly. Shop Passive Muffs → Electronic Ear Muffs NRR 22–28 Electronic muffs combine protection with awareness for optimal communication in the field and on the range. They block harmful noise while amplifying safe sounds. Best for instructors, frequent shooters, and range environments like competition or training. Shop Electronic Muffs → Electronic In-Ear NRR 18–25 Electronic ear plugs are the newest and most advanced option available and also come with the most features. Bluetooth, directional hearing, low-profile fit. Ideal for competition shooters and tactical use where mobility and spatial awareness are critical. Shop Electronic In-Ear → Best Ear Protection by Shooting Context Indoor Range Foam plugs + electronic muffs The most hazardous environment due to sound reflection. Doubling up is strongly recommended. Even if muffs are knocked off during training, plugs provide a last line of defense. Outdoor Range Electronic muffs or plugs NRR 22+ Sound dissipates more naturally, but gunshot reports remain potentially damaging. Electronic options give protection while maintaining communication and spatial awareness. Competition Shooting Electronic in-ear plugs Speed and awareness are top priorities. Rapid physical movement and sweat moisture are additional factors. Electronic in-ear provides secure fit, low profile, and clear hearing of range officer commands. Tactical / LE Training Electronic in-ear with Bluetooth / comms Communication and situational awareness are critical. These systems allow seamless team coordination while protecting hearing and enabling directional awareness for early threat detection. NRR Ratings Explained — How Much Protection Do You Actually Need? The Noise Reduction Rating (NRR) tells you how much sound a device can block, but real-world performance can be lower than advertised. NRR Rating Formula Real-World Reduction NRR 22 (22 – 7) ÷ 2 ~7.5 dB NRR 25 (25 – 7) ÷ 2 ~9 dB NRR 28 (28 – 7) ÷ 2 ~10.5 dB NRR 33 (33 – 7) ÷ 2 ~13 dB This is why higher NRR and sometimes doubling up can be necessary and a best practice. Doubling Up — When and How to Wear Plugs + Muffs Doubling up means wearing ear plugs + ear muffs together. When to Do It Indoor ranges Shooting high-caliber rifles Long shooting sessions Important: NRR values don't stack directly. Instead, add about +5 dB to the higher-rated protection. Also consider that hearing protection can be uncomfortable and there is an adjustment period when someone is new to shooting. New shooters should make it a point to wear hearing protection before going to the range to get used to the slight discomfort in a non-hazardous noise environment. FAQ What is the best ear protection for shooting? This depends greatly on the environment. Indoor ranges require maximum protection (doubling up), while outdoor and competition shooting benefit from electronic options. Hearing protection should be tested off the range beforehand and phased into gradually, starting with smaller caliber firearms. Consideration should be made for the level of training, type of firearm, and environment. How much ear protection do I need for shooting? Outdoor: Minimum NRR 22. Indoor: NRR 28+ (preferably doubled). The more hazardous the environment, the higher the protection required. Can shooting damage hearing with ear protection? Yes, if your protection is insufficient for the noise level or not worn correctly. Damage can also occur if hearing protection is unintentionally moved out of place during live-fire training or competition. Are electronic ear muffs worth it? Absolutely. They allow you to hear conversations and commands while still protecting your hearing. They also provide next-gen options like text and phone call communications, as well as music playback (not recommended during live-fire training). The Axil MXII Pro covers all of the needs for recreational and competition shooting and is used around the world by experienced shooters needing optimal performance and protection. Conclusion Choosing the best ear protection for shooting has different factors, but matching your gear to your environment should be heavily considered. Indoor ranges → maximum protection (double up) Outdoor shooting → balance protection and awareness Competition/tactical → prioritize communication and mobility Modern options — especially electronic hearing protection like the Axil MXII or the XCOR Pro — make it easier than ever to stay safe without sacrificing performance. Having the best ear protection for the job allows shooters to maximize training value and optimize performance in competition. For professionals in law enforcement the stakes can be much higher. The information in this guide can assist all levels of shooters make the best decision to cover their needs and ensure the best protection, regardless of the environment.

title: Isabella Bank Announces Promotion of Dee Powell to Company Officer
summary: Isabella Bank Chief Operations Officer Erika Ross announced the promotion of Dee Powell to bank officer.
body_text: Isabella Bank Chief Operations Officer Erika Ross announced the promotion of Dee Powell to bank officer. Powell serves as a project manager and is based at the bank’s main office in downtown Mount Pleasant. As project manager, Powell is responsible for managing the Bank’s project portfolio while supporting project owners. Her role ensures projects align with the Bank’s mission and follow a comprehensive process that supports safety and soundness. “Powell has served Isabella Bank for more than a decade in a variety of roles,” Ross said. “Her diverse background has prepared her with the expertise needed to manage projects as we continue to advance the Bank’s mission. This is a well-deserved promotion.” Powell joined Isabella Bank in 2013 as a teller and was later promoted to supervisor and branch manager of the Remus branch. She transitioned to the operations team as digital banking manager before becoming project manager. Powell earned a Bachelor of Arts in psychology from the University of South Carolina and a Master of Business Administration from Central Michigan University. She is also a graduate of the Dale Carnegie Leadership program, Leadership Mecosta, and the Michigan Bankers Association’s Perry Schools of Banking. Community service is important to Powell. She volunteers with organizations including Junior Achievement, where she teaches financial literacy to area youth, and Special Olympics Michigan. She also serves as vice president of the Remus Area Downtown Development Authority and volunteers with the annual Remus Heritage Days Festival, God’s Helping Hands, and St. Michael Catholic Church and School. “Community banking holds a special place for me, as I have always been engaged in the communities where I work and live to ensure we are bettering the future for our children and others who come after us,” Powell said. “When our communities succeed, we succeed right alongside them by assisting with their financial well-being and long-term growth.” Powell was born and raised in central Michigan. She now lives in Blanchard with her husband, Chris, and their three children, Croix, Daisy, and Demi. The Powell family enjoys outdoor activities, sports, friendly competition, and spending time together.

title: Innovation Meets Style: The One-of-One Radical AirFlow Looks at This Year’s Pre Classic
summary: At the premiere track event, 11 Nike athletes work custom apparel that served multiple purposes: Keep them cool, keep them confident, and unleash their speed.
body_text: In a sport decided by hundredths of a second, every edge matters, physical and mental alike. At this year’s Prefontaine Classic , where the world’s top track and field athletes were competing to be the fastest and best in their sport, one edge came in the form of custom warm-up apparel. Ask Masai Russell, who claimed the women’s 100-meter hurdles after warming up in Nike’s newest cooling innovation: a one-of-one Radical AirFlow garment designed specifically for her. The breathable material, which launched in trail running in 2025 and is now making its debut across the track, court and beyond , is built to harness airflow and maximize the body’s natural cooling system. “I was astonished, because I’d seen the Radical AirFlow material and felt the texture before,” says Masai, “but actually trying it on and seeing it here in real life, in the flesh, was insane. I was so impressed by the feel.” She wasn’t the only one. Eleven Nike athletes wore bespoke Radical AirFlow tops at Pre, including Tara Davis-Woodhall, who took the W for the women's long jump, and Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, who won the women’s 100 meters. Designed with each athlete’s event and sense of style in mind, the garments served multiple purposes: Keep them cool, keep them confident, and unleash their speed.
